title: Helping Reticent Team Members Find the Courage to Speak Up
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses why some team members struggle to voice their views even in psychologically safe environments: they haven't consciously articulated a reason compelling enough to override their reticence. The author offers a long list of candidate reasons a leader can surface for a hesitant colleague — from role obligation to fear of regret to protecting others from unfair outcomes — and argues that simply naming these reasons, plus prompting reflection on the cost of silence, is often enough to unlock participation. The piece closes by adding 'reminder' to the list of roles a good leader plays alongside conductor, coach, and director.
points: Team members who struggle to speak up often simply lack a clear, internalized reason for doing so — not confidence in general.
Leaders can help by supplying a menu of concrete reasons to speak up (role obligation, care for outcomes, avoiding future regret, protecting others from unfairness).
Prompting reticent colleagues to think through the consequences of staying silent is often what unlocks their willingness to contribute.
The leader's job includes being a 'reminder' — not just a director or coach — of the reasons people already have for engaging.
quotes: Finding the courage to advocate, contribute, or opine on an issue or in a given situation is not always easy. People must have a good reason to expose their candid views to others.
Good leaders remind those who lack the courage to share their candid views of the many good reasons they have for speaking up.
Reticent colleagues often haven’t thought through the many reasons they should speak up.
They encourage others to think about the consequences of remaining silent.
Good leaders are not only conductors, orchestrators, educators, and directors. They are also reminders.
